readerTitle: Why a $1 trinket sold for far more with a story attached
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Significant Objects 프로젝트, Small·Loewenstein·Slovic 2007 기부 실험) + 가상 적용 (콜드체인 용기 제조사, 병원 예약 소프트웨어)
insight: 사실은 고객이 믿게 만들고, 이야기는 고객이 그 사실을 떠올리게 만든다. 그래서 숫자를 앞세우기보다 구체적인 한 사람의 변화를 먼저 보여주고 숫자로 뒷받침한다.
misconception: 숫자와 사양을 더 많이 보여줄수록 설득력이 커진다. 이야기는 감성적인 소비재에만 통하고 B2B나 기술 제품에는 필요 없다.

sources.text: Walker, R. & Glenn, J. Significant Objects project (2009), and the book Significant Objects (2012)

Small, D. A., Loewenstein, G. & Slovic, P. (2007). Sympathy and callousness: The impact of deliberative thought on donations to identifiable and statistical victims. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 102(2), 143–153.
콜드체인 용기 제조사, 병원 예약 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Significant Objects 1차 시즌: 물건 100개 구입 총액 약 $128.74, eBay 판매 총액 약 $3,612.51로 알려져 있음. 게시 전 프로젝트 사이트나 책에서 정확한 수치와 물건 개수를 다시 확인하세요. 배수 계산: 3,612.51 ÷ 128.74 ≈ 28.1배.
Significant Objects 경매 목록에 이야기가 창작(fiction)이라는 점이 표시되었다는 내용을 확인하세요. 통제된 실험이 아니었고 언론 노출 효과가 섞였을 수 있다는 점은 7번 카드에 적었습니다.
Small et al. (2007) 연구 1: 참가자가 받은 $5 중 평균 기부액. 개인(Rokia) 이야기 약 $2.38, 통계 정보 약 $1.14, 이야기+통계 약 $1.43. 원문 표로 수치를 다시 확인하세요. '약 2배' 표현은 2.38 ÷ 1.14 ≈ 2.1배 기준.

cards.title: Why a $1 trinket sold for far more with a story attached
body: In 2009, two writers, Rob Walker and Joshua Glenn, bought about 100 cheap objects from thrift stores. A plastic figure, an old mug, a souvenir. Most cost a dollar or two.

They asked writers to invent a short story for each one, then listed them on eBay with the story attached. The whole batch cost about $129. Nothing about the objects changed. Only the words next to them did.

image.label: A cheap thrift-store figurine next to a handwritten story card
image.brief: 중고 가게 선반 위의 작은 플라스틱 인형 하나. 옆에 "$1" 가격표, 그 앞에 손글씨 이야기 카드가 놓여 있음. 따뜻한 조명, 3D 클레이 스타일. 실제 브랜드나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Your container keeps vaccines cold. How do you open the brochure?
body: You make insulated shipping containers for medicine distributors. Your container holds 2–8°C for 96 hours, longer than most rivals.
You have one page to win a logistics manager's attention. What goes at the top?

options.text: The full spec table: hold time, weight, test results
options.feedback: Accurate and needed, but it reads like every other brochure on the desk. Specs win the comparison later; they rarely win the first look.

options.text: A real customer: a shipment stuck in customs for three days that arrived still in range, then the spec
options.feedback: The story makes "96 hours" mean something the manager can picture and repeat to the boss. The spec right after it backs the story up.
It sounds warm but says nothing a rival couldn't say. You trade your real advantage for a nice phrase.

cards.title: Same objects. About 28 times the money.
body: The stories were clearly made-up fiction, and buyers knew it. They paid about **$3,600** in total anyway.

cards.title: Storytelling
body: **Storytelling** in marketing means showing a specific person, the problem they faced, and what changed. Facts tell people what is true. A story lets them picture it happening.

A pictured event is easier to remember and easier to retell. The logistics manager won't repeat "96-hour hold time" in a meeting. They will repeat "the shipment that sat in customs for three days and was fine."

image.label: Three panels: a person, a problem, a change
image.brief: 세 칸 만화형 인포그래픽. 1칸 "Someone" (물류 담당자), 2칸 "A problem" (세관에 멈춘 화물과 달력 3일), 3칸 "What changed" (온도계 정상 범위 체크 표시). 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Adding statistics made a story weaker.
body: In a 2007 study, researchers gave people $5 and asked them to donate to a children's charity. Some read about one girl, Rokia. Others read statistics about millions of children in need.
The Rokia group gave about **twice as much** on average. When Rokia's story came with the statistics attached, giving dropped back toward the lower level.
The lesson for business isn't to hide numbers. It's to lead with one clear case and let the numbers support it, not bury it.

cards.title: A useful story fits in four lines.
body: Most customer stories that work follow the same simple shape:
list: **Before:** who the customer is and what normal looked like
**Problem:** the moment it went wrong, with a real detail
**Turn:** what your product or service did
**After:** the result, in their numbers if possible
cards.callout: A bakery's catering order, a plumber's emergency call or a software rollout all fit this shape.

cards.title: A story earns attention, not trust.
body: Significant Objects was a fun project, not a controlled experiment. Buyers knew the stories were fiction, and the press coverage likely helped prices.
In real selling, your story must be true and typical. A one-in-a-thousand success presented as normal will be found out, and buyers who feel misled rarely come back.
Business buyers will still check the spec, the price and the terms. The story gets you read. The facts get you chosen.

cards.title: Now it's booking software for clinics.
body: Your app lets patients book and reschedule by text. One dental clinic told you missed appointments fell sharply after switching, and their receptionist stopped dreading Monday mornings.
What leads your homepage's customer section?

options.feedback: Good proof that you're safe, but it's the same line every competitor uses. Keep it nearby as support.

options.text: The receptionist's story: the Monday phone rush, the switch, and the clinic's own no-show numbers
options.feedback: Clinic owners see their own front desk in it, and the real numbers keep it honest. Ask permission and use their words.
It looks thorough, but visitors must work out the benefit themselves. Most won't.

cards.softwareNote: For software, the strongest stories usually come from support tickets and sales calls. Save the exact moments customers describe, with permission to quote them.

cards.title: Lead with one real customer. Back it with numbers.
body: People remember a specific person and what changed for them. Facts then make the story believable.
**Try it today:** pick one happy customer. Write four lines: before, problem, turn, after. Put it at the top of your next pitch or brochure.
